newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - New supply, second-tier data.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - New supply, second-tier data.

text.p: A dose of fresh supply will steal the spotlight in the U.S. fixed-income market on Tuesday, overshadowing several second-tier data releases, analysts said.
The Treasury will auction $8.0 billion of index-linked 10-year notes Tuesday, and about $3.0 billion of high-grade corporate debt is expected to be issued during the week.
Treasuries posted moderate gains amid short-covering on Monday, and the gentle upswing could continue if supply does not weigh too heavily, analysts said.
"We're just watching flows and keeping tabs on sentiment," said Lee Youngdahl, vice president and bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc.
Although the indexed note auction is expected to go well, the Treasury's second-ever installment of the issue could suffer from higher market interest rates, which make other securities attractive.

"With market rates backing up, you may see some of the people who were interested in the inflation-indexed bond three months ago no longer interested in the next round," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
On the flip side, however, future inflation fears may run deep enough to bolster demand for the securities despite higher rates and expectations of further Fed tightenings.
"If inflation fears are rising, (indexed notes) should be relatively attractive," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
The notes auction alone should not overburden the long end of the curve, assuming the notes are placed reasonably well, analyst said.
On January 27, the Treasury sold its first run of $7.0 billion of 10-year inflation indexes notes at a yield of 3.449 percent, below projections of 3.51 to 3.52 percent.
But a few billion dollars of new corporate bonds may siphon flows from Treasuries as the week unfolds, they said.
In particular, JC Penney could launch its $2.0 billion multi-tranche offering as early as Tuesday, syndicate sources said.
Other deals that could price this week include a $1.0 billion, 10-year issue for the Asian Development Bank.
Only minor economic data are set for release Tuesday, and the market should pay those reports little heed.

A seasonal bug should pop up in both the BTM/Schroders chain store sales report, set for 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, and the Redbook Research retail sales release, scheduled for 1455 EDT/1855 GMT, analysts said.

The combination of Good Friday and Easter Sunday will depress the results for the week ended April 5, providing a test for both reports' seasonal adjustments. BTM/Schroders rose 0.6 percent in the week ended March 29, and Redbook climbed 0.8 percent in March versus February.
"The interesting thing tomorrow will be how distorted the sales data may be," said Sanwa's Strauss.
Gary Stern, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, addresses a community conference in Duluth, Minnesota, but he is scheduled to deliver a speech already well-digested by the market.
"I wouldn't imagine the things he's going to hit on would be too different. Tight labor markets, Fed vigilant against inflation, that type of thing," Lanston's Youngdahl said.
